name: Arisai
title: Son of Haman
summary: Arisai was one of Haman's ten sons. Haman, referred to as an Agagite, was the foremost enemy of the Jewish people in the Persian Empire during King Ahasuerus' reign. The conflict was triggered when Mordecai, the Jew, refused to bow down before Haman, and Haman sought to destroy the entire Jewish people in revenge. When the king's counter-decree gave the Jews the right to defend themselves against those who sought to annihilate them, Arisai was killed along with all his brothers on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar. At Queen Esther's request, the bodies of the ten sons were publicly hanged as a sign of the final judgment upon Haman's house. Their downfall marked the turning point in the story of Esther and forms an essential part of the foundation for the annual festival of Purim, where Jews celebrate their deliverance from destruction. In a broader biblical context, the fall of Haman's house reflects the ancient enmity between Israel and Amalek.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Exaltation
keyEvents.description: Haman was exalted by King Ahasuerus to the highest position among all the princes, setting the stage for the coming conflict with the Jews.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Plan to Destroy the Jews
keyEvents.description: Haman, the father of Arisai, devised a plan to destroy all the Jews in the Persian Empire after Mordecai refused to bow down to him.

keyEvents.title: Esther's Intercession
keyEvents.description: Queen Esther risked her life by going to the king uninvited to expose Haman's evil plot and save her people.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Execution
keyEvents.description: Haman was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai, marking the beginning of the downfall of his entire household.

keyEvents.title: Arisai and His Brothers Are Killed
keyEvents.description: Arisai was killed along with his nine brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar—the date originally set by Haman's decree for the destruction of the Jews. The ten sons of Haman are mentioned by name.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Sons Are Hanged
keyEvents.description: At Esther's request, King Ahasuerus ordered that the ten dead sons of Haman, including Arisai, be hanged on gallows as a public sign of judgment against the enemies of the Jews.

versions.summary: Arisai was one of the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, an enemy of the Jews in the Persian Empire. He was killed along with his brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies following King Ahasuerus' decree. His death marked the complete destruction of Haman's household and is part of the background for the festival of Purim.

versions.reason: [major] The Roles field is empty. Arisai should have at least one role, such as "Son of Haman" or similar, to provide context for the profile.; [major] Arisai is included in his own sibling list. He should be removed from the siblings array. Additionally, the correct number of siblings is missing: Haman had ten sons, and Arisai is one of them, so there should be nine siblings. The list also lacks the siblings with correct IDs. According to Est 9:7-9, the ten sons are: Parshandata, Dalfon, Aspata, Porata, Adalja, Aridata, Parmashta, Arisai, Vajesata, and the tenth is Aridai. The list is missing 'Aridai'.; [minor] The description says "Haman's father was exalted" but it was Haman himself who was exalted, not his father. This is a factual error.; [minor] The description says "his nine brothers" but Arisai had nine brothers (ten sons in total). The phrasing is correct in itself, but the important point is that the list of siblings in the family field must be corrected to include all nine.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. The profile should have notes on, for example, the Hebrew name, the Purim tradition of reading aloud the names of the sons, or historical-linguistic details about the Agagites.; [minor] The summary is good but could be clarified slightly: it was not just a defensive decree, but a counter-decree that allowed the Jews to defend themselves.

versions.reason: [minor] The lifespan is given as 'approx. 4th century BC' but the events in the book of Esther are traditionally linked to Xerxes I (Ahasverus) who reigned approx. 486–465 BC. It would be more accurate to state 'approx. 5th century BC' or 'approx. 500s BC'.; [minor] The summary is well formulated, but since this is version 2, it should be further differentiated from version 1. This can be strengthened by clarifying the theological dimension of the Amalek conflict and God's providence in the Esther narrative.; [minor] The description says 'the thirteenth day of the month Adar'. According to Esth 9:1 and 9:17, the battle took place on the thirteenth day, while the Jews rested on the fourteenth. This is correct, but it can be clarified that this was the date set by Haman's original decree.

footnotes.text: The name Arisai (Hebrew: אֲרִיסַי) has an uncertain etymology but is thought to be of Persian origin. Some scholars have suggested a connection to Old Iranian words, reflecting the Persian cultural context of Haman's family at the court in Susa.

In Jewish Purim tradition, the names of Haman's ten sons are read aloud in a single breath during the reading of the Book of Esther (Megillat Esther), to signify that they were all killed simultaneously. This custom is preserved in rabbinic literature (Talmud, Megillah 16b). The names are also written in a special, enlarged column in Hebrew scrolls.

The designation "Agagite" regarding Haman has been the subject of considerable discussion. Many scholars link this to Agag, king of the Amalekites (1 Sam 15), placing the conflict between Haman and Mordecai within a broader biblical context of enmity between Israel and Amalek—a conflict that extends from Exod 17 throughout the Old Testament.

The Persian names of Haman's ten sons may reflect historical ties to the Persian aristocracy. Archaeological finds from Persepolis and Susa have confirmed the use of similar Persian names in this period, and inscriptions from the Achaemenid era reveal a diverse, multilingual society at the Persian court.

The events in the Book of Esther take place in the Persian capital Susa (Hebrew: שׁוּשָׁן), identified with the archaeological site of Shush in southwestern Iran. French excavations from the 19th century uncovered large palace structures that match the descriptions of Ahasuerus's court in the Book of Esther.
